desc:
Every element of nums is 0, 1 or 2. In one move you may swap any two elements. Return the minimum number of moves needed to sort the array in non-decreasing order.

nums = [2, 1, 0]
result = 1
nums = [1, 2, 0]
result = 2

In the second example no single swap works: all three elements are out of place and they are rotated cyclically.
hints: The sorted target is known: it is determined by how many 0s, 1s and 2s there are. Compare each position with the value it should hold.
Count the misplaced positions by pair: c[a][b] = positions that should hold a but hold b. A single swap fixes two positions when it exchanges a (a, b) position with a (b, a) position.

First match as many such pairs as possible: min(c[a][b], c[b][a]) for each of the three pairs of values, each costing 1 swap. The positions that remain form 3-cycles (like 0 → 1 → 2 → 0) and every 3-cycle needs 2 swaps.
editorial: Let the sorted array be t. For each position with nums[i] != t[i] record the pair (t[i], nums[i]), meaning 'wants t[i], has nums[i]'. There are six pair types. A swap of positions of type (a, b) and (b, a) repairs both at the cost of one swap, and no swap can repair more than two positions, so we should take as many such 2-cycles as possible: min(c[a][b], c[b][a]) for each pair of values.

After removing these matches, what remains is balanced (every value leaves as many positions as it fills) and for each of the three value pairs only one direction survives. The leftover must therefore decompose into cycles (0,1) (1,2) (2,0) or (0,2) (2,1) (1,0), each of three misplaced positions. A 3-cycle needs exactly 2 swaps. If r positions are left, the cost is 2 * r / 3.

Counting takes one pass, so the algorithm is O(n) time and O(1) space. The total answer is pairs + 2 * (remaining / 3). Sorting and counting inversions would be wrong here: swaps may exchange any two elements, not only neighbours.
